analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor, the bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and received no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lock in permanently the income tax cuts from 2001, the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividends from 2003, and the repeal of the estate tax, retroactive to the end of 2009. The estate tax applies only to very large estates, so its repeal would benefit a small number of the wealthiest families. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates (the estate tax applies only to estates worth millions), and high-income investors, who would keep the lowest rates on capital gains and dividends permanently.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of large estates and high-income investors

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the provisions of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 by repealing its scheduled sunset.
Makes permanent the reduced income tax rates on dividends and capital gains from the 2003 tax law by repealing their scheduled expiration.
Reinstates the repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, applying retroactively to deaths and gifts on or after December 31, 2009.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury — the revenue that the expiring tax cuts and the estate tax would have brought in would instead be lost, adding to deficits that fall later on general taxpayers. Within the tax code, ordinary wage earners gain little, because the provisions that most help top brackets are the ones the bill makes permanent.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax affects only very large estates, so its repeal concentrates the entire benefit on a small number of the wealthiest families while removing a significant revenue source, adding to federal deficits.
The bill would have made the tax cuts permanent without any offsetting revenue, meaning the cost would eventually fall on general taxpayers through higher debt or later tax increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated: heirs of multi-million-dollar estates and top-bracket investors gain the most, while the revenue loss adds to national debt that everyone eventually bears. There is no cost-offset or trade-off in the bill to balance this.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil Gingrey introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's passage, because it never advanced. Because it died, the estate tax remained on the books under the 2010 tax deal, and large estates stayed taxable.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died in committee

for.name: Rep. Phil Gingrey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeal the estate tax.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: The only support was two Republicans (the sponsor and one cosponsor); no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Repealing the estate tax, retroactive to the end of 2009, would transfer billions in avoided taxes to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates, funded by a loss of federal revenue that everyone else eventually bears.
Locking in the low 2003 rates on capital gains and dividends permanently preserves a tax rate that flows overwhelmingly to households with large investment income.
